claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the baseline alloy indicate dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
Micro-segregation causes the baseline alloy's significantly reduced room-temperature fracture strain.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 4 at.% Cr.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr induces a C14 or C15 multicomponent Laves phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The Cr-induced Laves phase has a volume fraction of approximately 4%.
The Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected morphology at grain boundaries and interdendritic regions.
The interconnected Laves-phase network impedes crack extension by causing crack deflection, branching, and pinning.
Cr has sufficient atomic-size mismatch with the BCC matrix to induce significant lattice distortion.
Cr-induced lattice distortion increases lattice friction and produces solid-solution hardening.
Cr addition contracts the BCC matrix lattice parameter relative to the Cr-free baseline.
The combination of the Laves-phase network and Cr solid-solution effects increases yield strength.
The combination of the Laves-phase network and Cr solid-solution effects increases fracture strain relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy's fracture strain will exceed the theoretical expectation for the segregated single-phase system.
HfNbTiVZr thin films deposited at 450 degrees Celsius can form a BCC matrix with C15 Laves-phase precipitates.
Microstructural heterogeneity can provide strength-ductility synergy in high- and medium-entropy alloys.
Failure of the BCC lattice parameter to contract invalidates the proposed Cr solid-solution-hardening mechanism.
Selection between C14 and C15 structures may depend on Cr diffusivity relative to Nb or Ta.
